3499793.background: Hamilton votes October 26, 2026 under first-past-the-post. Andrea Horwath, former Ontario NDP leader, won in 2022 by a narrow margin over Bob Bratina; Keanin Loomis, ex-Chamber of Commerce president, finished third. Strong-mayor powers, tax increases, LRT and housing dominate. Whether Horwath seeks re-election is a key unknown.

actors.name: Keanin Loomis
actors.public: Business-friendly centrist, former Hamilton Chamber of Commerce CEO; ran in 2022 and placed third; message centered on competence, taxes and economic development.
actors.private: Needs a consolidated centre-right vote and probably needs Horwath out or weakened; would avoid a multi-candidate split with another conservative-leaning contender.

actors.name: Andrea Horwath
actors.public: Incumbent mayor with high name recognition and progressive base; criticized over tax levy increases and use of strong-mayor powers, which she has said she dislikes.
actors.private: Could retire or seek another role; if she runs, incumbency and union/NDP machine make her the default favourite in a split field.

actors.name: Other centre-right candidates (e.g. Bratina-type figures)
actors.public: Former officials or councillors appealing to suburban and older voters frustrated with taxes and downtown issues.
actors.private: Their entry splits the anti-incumbent vote; each prefers to run rather than defer, which hurts the strongest challenger.

actors.name: Hamilton electorate
actors.public: Turnout in municipal races is low (~30-35%); suburban wards (Stoney Creek, Ancaster, Flamborough) lean conservative, lower city leans progressive.
actors.private: Affordability and property-tax anger is the main swing driver; low turnout favours organized bases.

events.name: Horwath does not seek re-election
Another major centre-right candidate enters and splits the vote
Major municipal scandal or tax-shock story in final weeks

3501950.background: IMF Portwatch normally records roughly 100-130 daily transit calls through Hormuz. A 60-call 7-day average threshold implies traffic was severely depressed by mid-2026, presumably from a US/Israel-Iran conflict, attacks or insurance withdrawal. I lack details of the 2026 disruption; recovery depends on a durable ceasefire and insurer/shipowner confidence.

actors.name: Iran (IRGC Navy)
actors.public: Has repeatedly threatened to close or harass Hormuz shipping; seized tankers in 2019 and 2023-24; uses mines, drones and fast boats.
actors.private: Full closure hurts its own exports and Chinese ties; prefers calibrated harassment as leverage; would ease if strikes on it stop and sanctions relief appears.

actors.name: United States and allied navies
actors.public: Commit to freedom of navigation; escort operations and strikes on Iranian assets are available tools.
actors.private: Want oil prices down before US midterms; willing to escort and pressure Tehran, but avoid an open-ended war.

actors.name: Shipowners and war-risk insurers
actors.public: Follow Joint War Committee listed-area designations; premiums spike and many operators pause transits after attacks.
actors.private: Return slowly, typically weeks after hostilities end; need several incident-free weeks before volumes normalize.

actors.name: Gulf exporters (Saudi, UAE, Qatar)
actors.public: Need Hormuz open for oil and LNG; have limited bypass pipelines (East-West, Habshan-Fujairah).
actors.private: Quietly lobby Washington and Tehran for de-escalation; Qatar LNG has no bypass and strongly wants normal traffic.

events.name: Durable ceasefire or US-Iran deal announced
New attack or mining incident on commercial shipping
Portwatch data revision or reporting gap

3502066.background: A November 2024 ceasefire ended the Israel-Hezbollah war; Israel keeps five positions in south Lebanon and keeps striking. A US-led 'mechanism' meets at Naqoura; in December 2025 both states added civilian envoys (Simon Karam, Uri Resnick), creating direct in-person talks. Washington pushes Hezbollah disarmament.

actors.name: Israeli government
actors.public: Demands Hezbollah disarmament, keeps hilltop positions, strikes frequently; welcomes direct talks and economic cooperation framing.
actors.private: Values direct meetings as normalization step; will keep attending mechanism sessions as long as they legitimize its security demands.

actors.name: Lebanese government (Aoun, Salam)
actors.public: Committed to state monopoly on arms; agreed to civilian representatives in mechanism; rejects normalization.
actors.private: Will accept technical/security talks to get Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction money; constrained by Hezbollah and Shia public; avoids anything looking like peace treaty.

actors.name: United States (envoys, CENTCOM)
actors.public: Chairs the mechanism; envoys like Ortagus/Barrack pressure Beirut on disarmament timelines.
actors.private: Wants regular visible meetings as foreign-policy wins; can convene sessions at short notice.

actors.name: Hezbollah
actors.public: Refuses disarmament north of Litani, denounces direct talks as normalization.
actors.private: Weak militarily; will not topple the government over talks but can pressure Shia ministers to slow them.

events.name: Mechanism session at Naqoura held in the window
Major Israel-Hezbollah escalation suspending talks
Lebanese cabinet crisis over disarmament

actors.private: Low priority versus other issues; might use a release as distraction before midterms; needs agencies to produce reviewed material.

actors.private: Prefers controlled releases of mundane resolved cases; resists exposing sensitive sensor capabilities.

actors.name: ODNI (Tulsi Gabbard)

actors.private: Could quickly release a tranche to generate publicity; bandwidth constrained by other priorities.

events.name: AARO publishes new case resolutions or videos

Executive order or directive on UAP disclosure
